fields.hook: Between 2011–12 and 2022–23, the share of people in Northern Ireland reporting very low anxiety rose from 34.11% to 39.53%, while it fell in the other three UK nations.
fields.summary: Northern Ireland moved from 4th of the four UK nations in 2011–12 to the highest share of people reporting very low anxiety in 2022–23. The share peaked at 46.95% in 2017–18 and is now 7.42 percentage points below that peak. Average anxiety, happiness and worthwhile scores also improved over the same period.
fields.body_md:
Northern Ireland is the only UK nation where the share of people reporting very low anxiety rose between 2011–12 and 2022–23. It went from 34.11% to 39.53%, a rise of 5.42 percentage points, according to the Office for National Statistics' annual personal well-being estimates. Very low anxiety means that people rated how anxious they felt the day before at the very bottom of the scale.

Northern Ireland started 4th of the four nations on this measure and ended 1st. In 2022–23 it had the highest share of the four, at 39.53%, clearly above Scotland's 35.81%. That is a striking turnaround for a nation that began the period behind the rest of the UK.

## A rise, then a fall

The rise was not steady. The share climbed year after year to a peak of 46.95% in 2017–18. It then fell by 5.85 percentage points in a single year, to 41.1% in 2018–19. In 2020–21 it dipped again, from 40.54% to 35.94%, a fall of 4.6 percentage points. That dip was shared across the UK: all four nations saw the share fall in 2020–21.

By 2021–22 the share in Northern Ireland had recovered to 39.71%, and in 2022–23 it was 39.53%. That latest figure is still 7.42 percentage points below the 2017–18 peak of 46.95%, so the gains made up to 2017–18 have not fully returned. The overall rise is real, but the recent picture is flatter than the early years suggested.

## How it compares

Elsewhere in the UK, the picture went the other way. In Scotland, the share reporting very low anxiety fell from 38.41% in 2011–12 to 35.81% in 2022–23. In Wales it fell from 38.5% to 35.01%. England also ended the period lower than it started. Across the four nations, the median change was a fall of 2.42 percentage points, against a rise of 5.42 in Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland's rise was the biggest of the four nations.

The other well-being measures for Northern Ireland moved in the same, better direction. Average anxiety fell from 3.15 to 2.91 out of 10, where a lower score is better. Average anxiety reached its low point of 2.53 in 2017–18, the same year that very low anxiety peaked. Average happiness rose from 7.39 to 7.57 out of 10. The average score for feeling that the things you do in life are worthwhile rose from 7.76 to 7.93. Each of these changes is clear of the survey's margin of error. They are smaller than the shift in very low anxiety, but they point the same way.

## What the data can't tell us

These are survey estimates, not counts of every person. Each figure has a confidence interval: for Northern Ireland in 2022–23, the share with very low anxiety is estimated at between 37.74% and 41.32%. In 2011–12 the range was 31.96% to 36.27%. The ranges for the start and end years do not overlap, which is why the rise can be called clear, but small moves from one year to the next may not be real changes.

The survey records how people rated their own feelings. It does not say why more people in Northern Ireland reported very low anxiety, or why fewer did elsewhere, so the data cannot link the change to any policy, event or to the pandemic.

ONS paused its annual personal well-being estimates after April 2022 to March 2023 because of falling response rates and weighting problems in the Annual Population Survey, so 2022–23 is the latest year available. Since October 2024, ONS has classed these estimates as official statistics in development rather than accredited official statistics. The figures should be read with some caution, and this story will be updated if ONS publishes newer annual data.

The numbers come from the Office for National Statistics dataset Personal well-being estimates by local authority, covering 2011–12 to 2022–23.

prompt.instructions:
You are writing a short data story for DataTales (datatales.co.uk), a UK site
that turns public data into plain, accurate stories. Python has already done all
the maths; your job is only the words around the numbers below.

Rules (follow every one):
1. Use ONLY numbers that appear in NUMBERS or CHART DATA below. Do not calculate new
   numbers (no new differences, ratios, averages or percentages) and do not round to a
   different figure than one you could get by rounding a number given. Years must be within
   the data period (years mentioned in `caveats` are also allowed).
2. UK English. Plain, calm language for a general reader. No hype words ("shocking",
   "soaring", "plummeting", "crisis"). Write financial years with an en dash: 2011–12.
3. HEADLINE: state the single strongest finding as a statement with its key fact, e.g.
   "Northern Ireland is the only UK nation where low anxiety rose". Never a topic label
   such as "Wellbeing in Northern Ireland 2011–2023".
4. FRAMING: `chart_facts.supported_checks` lists what the chart data clearly supports
   (only_rise, only_fall, all_rise, all_fall, highest, lowest, biggest_rise, biggest_fall).
   When one is supported, prefer that framing ("the only nation where…", "the biggest rise
   of the four…"), or rank-change framing from `rank_change`/`overtook` in the findings.
5. Every change or gap in NUMBERS is statistically clear (confidence intervals do not
   overlap). Say "clearly higher/lower" if useful; never say "significant".
6. Respect polarity: `higher_is_better` and `good_news` say whether a rise is good. For
   anxiety, a LOWER score is better. Band labels for anxiety mean: Poor = high anxiety,
   Fair = medium, Good = low, Very good = very low anxiety. Never write "very good anxiety";
   write "very low anxiety".
7. When `unit` starts with "%", a change in `change` is in percentage points: write
   "5.42 percentage points", never "5.42%". `pct_change` is a relative change. Write every
   percentage with exactly 2 decimals: 38.50%, 5.00% (never 38.5% or 39%).
8. SHAPE: `series[].points` has every year and `series[].peak` the peak and low point. If
   `latest_well_below_peak` is true, say plainly that the latest value is well below the
   peak, with both numbers and years. Mention notable dips or rises from `notable_moves` and
   `moves_shared_by_most_geographies` (for example 2020–21) briefly, with their numbers. If
   they are empty, do not invent one.
9. STRUCTURE of body_md (500 to 700 words): first the main finding and its shape; then
   "## How it compares" (the other geographies and the other measures in NUMBERS); then
   "## What the data can't tell us" (these are survey estimates with confidence intervals;
   the data does not explain causes; and every point in `caveats`, such as the paused annual
   release). Say where the data comes from (source name) and the period covered.
10. RANK WORDS: use "only", "all", "highest", "lowest", "biggest" or "largest" only for the
   charted measure, and only when a check proves it (rule 11). Otherwise avoid these words.
11. CLAIMS: for EVERY sentence in any field that contains a number other than a year, or any
   of the rank words above, add one claim:
   {"sentence": <copied exactly>, "keys": [<KEYS used>], "checks": [<checks>]}.
   Each number must equal (after rounding) one of its keys. Each rank word needs a check of
   the matching kind: only -> only_rise/only_fall; all -> all_rise/all_fall; highest ->
   highest; lowest -> lowest; biggest/largest -> biggest_rise/biggest_fall. Copy checks from
   `chart_facts.supported_checks` (without "detail"), or write one with other periods; every
   check is re-tested against chart_data. If the same sentence is used in two fields, one
   claim covers both. Count words like "four" as numbers. For a value from CHART DATA use
   the key chart.<geography>.<period>.value (or .lower / .upper for its confidence interval).
   Chart titles and annotations are checked like the other text: keep numbers out of them
   unless they come from the data, and give any such sentence a claim.
12. CHARTS: chart_spec is the main chart (a line chart of every year suits most stories).
   `more_charts` may add up to 2 more from the same chart_data: "slope" (first vs last period,
   good for showing who rose and who fell) and "map" (one period by area; only for nations,
   regions or local authorities, and only when chart_data has a `code` column). Give each a
